claims.text: Formation of a metastable single-phase solid solution in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by competition between kinetic trapping and a thermodynamic drive for surface-energy minimization.
Rapid heating and cooling can produce a kinetically trapped, single-phase solid solution in nanoparticles containing more than five noble-metal elements.
Cooling rate and an isothermal hold just below the decomposition temperature constitute the controlled intervention.
A thermal window around 700–1000 °C permits sufficient atomic mobility for elemental redistribution.
Elements with lower surface energies preferentially migrate to and enrich the nanoparticle surface.
Evolution of local elemental distribution mediates the transition from a single-phase solid solution to a segregated or multiphase structure.
Rapid heating and cooling minimize atomic diffusion.
Suppression of diffusion by rapid thermal cycling kinetically traps a chemically uniform, single-phase structure.
Slower cooling or an intermediate hold increases diffusion and allows preferential elemental redistribution toward the nanoparticle surface.
Differences in elemental surface energies and decomposition enthalpies govern preferential surface segregation.
Preferential diffusion and surface segregation result in phase separation.
Thermally enabled redistribution can alter nanoparticle morphology.
Slow-cooled or isothermally held nanoparticles will show greater elemental segregation than rapidly quenched controls.
Slow-cooled or isothermally held nanoparticles will develop a multiphase microstructure.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain a metastable single-phase structure.
The hypothesis applies to noble metal–based nanoparticles containing more than five elements when surface-energy and decomposition-kinetic disparities are significant.
The mechanism may not apply when constituent surface energies and decomposition kinetics differ only minimally or when particle length scales fundamentally alter diffusion.
The required temperature, cooling rate, and hold duration depend on composition and nanoparticle size and remain unquantified.

Absence of a statistically significant increase in surface enrichment or phase separation after slow cooling and an isothermal hold relative to a rapid-quench control would falsify the proposed cooling-induced diffusion mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes rapid, kinetically driven thermal decomposition as one side of the governing competition, whereas the mechanism, baseline, and prediction state that rapid heating and cooling suppress diffusion and preserve the single phase while slower treatment causes decomposition or phase separation. The meaning and role of 'rapid thermal decomposition' are therefore internally inconsistent.
